passage: Dear Diary, today at lunch break everyone crowded around Yusuf's new spectacles. Somebody started calling him 'Owl Eyes' and then like eight of us were saying it and hooting. I hooted too. Loud. It felt like my voice was mixed up with everyone's, so it didn't really count, and nobody was even looking at me. But when Yusuf took off his glasses and wiped them on his shirt and didn't look up, my stomach went funny. If it was only me and him, I would never say that. I don't even think owls are funny. Tomorrow I will sit next to him at lunch and say sorry, even if the others laugh. — Reena

qa.a: Somebody started calling him 'Owl Eyes' because of his new spectacles.

Then Seema's grandmother came round the corner with a bucket. Her eyes found Leela, only Leela. "You too, beti?" Leela's face went hot. The chant fell apart. She picked up the empty can and handed it back without a word.

"Pooja, come here a sec," Irfan said, pulling her into the stairwell of their building.

"They're just having fun."

"That's why. You turn the music down and bring out the cake. I'll ask them off the wall to light the sparklers."

Pooja laughed, a bit shakily. "Fine. Go."
Five minutes later the parapet was empty, and everyone was crowding around a lopsided chocolate cake.

passage: I'm Jagdish, and last month I learned something about crowds at our college fee protest. It started well: slogans, songs, Preeti with her hand-painted banner. By the time we reached the admin block, though, the chants had changed. Somebody started kicking the gate. A second-year boy picked up a brick 'just to hold'. I felt the pull too; my own voice was getting louder and meaner, and I didn't recognise the words coming out. That scared me more than the brick. I told Preeti, "This isn't us anymore." She looked around and nodded. We went to the front and started the slow song from the morning again. About thirty people joined. The brick went back on the ground. Looking back, noticing early was what mattered; ten minutes later, I don't think anyone would have listened.

grounding: Shows a student leader under fest pressure growing careless of juniors' feelings and bending rules for herself while believing she is unchanged.

passage: Three months into his internship at a design studio in Salt Lake, Anirban was asked to guide the two newest interns. He was pleased; he had always hated how the seniors ignored him. Within weeks, though, he was sending Jeevan back to redo slides at 7 p.m. while he left at six, "because I've done my hours." He started using the good corner desk everyone was supposed to share, and signed his own name at the bottom of a poster Jeevan had drawn most of. When Jeevan mentioned missing the last metro twice, Anirban said, "Welcome to the real world," and went back to his phone. On Friday he told his mother he was still the same easygoing Anirban from college. He didn't notice that she didn't answer.

qa.q: What did Anirban say when Jeevan mentioned missing the last metro?
qa.a: Anirban said, "Welcome to the real world," and went back to his phone.

qa.q: Why does Anirban believe nothing has changed?
qa.a: Anirban feels comfortable still seeing himself as the easygoing person from college, and is too wrapped up in his own hours to notice how Jeevan is affected.

qa.q: Which moment could have been a turning point for Anirban, and what could he do?
qa.a: When his mother didn't answer, Anirban could have asked why and looked honestly at the late slides, the corner desk and the poster credit.

qa.q: What would change if Anirban remembered how the seniors ignored him?
qa.a: Anirban might treat Jeevan the way he once wished to be treated: leaving on time, sharing the desk and giving credit for the poster.

grounding: Illustrates an intern with a little authority growing less attentive to a junior and taking perks, while believing he is the same person.

passage:
"Manoj bhaiya, you've been on the phone for an hour," Siddharth said, dropping onto the sofa.
"Mess committee stuff. The juniors messed up the Diwali menu." Manoj covered the phone, then spoke into it. "No, Aakash, I don't care if your exam is tomorrow. Redo the list tonight."
"He has an exam tomorrow?"
"Everyone has exams. I had exams too."
"You also got extra paneer from the mess every night last month. You told me."
"Secretary perk. Not a big deal."
"Last year you fought the old secretary for doing exactly that."
Manoj frowned. "That was different. He was arrogant."
"Bhaiya, you just told a junior you don't care."
"I said it nicely." Manoj looked down at his phone. "Didn't I?"
"You sounded like the old secretary."
"I'm the same person, Siddharth."
Siddharth shrugged and reached for the remote. "Okay. Just saying."

qa.q: What did Manoj say the juniors messed up?
qa.a: Manoj said the juniors messed up the Diwali menu.

qa.q: What does Manoj's "Didn't I?" suggest he is starting to feel?
qa.a: It suggests a flicker of doubt: for a moment Manoj wonders whether he really sounded harsh, though he still insists he's the same person 🤔

qa.q: What could Manoj do after that moment of doubt?
qa.a: Manoj could call Aakash back, let the list wait until after the exam, and give up the extra paneer.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the change in Manoj?
qa.a: Siddharth sees Manoj turning into the arrogant old secretary he once fought, taking perks and brushing off a junior's exam.

grounding: Shows a student mess secretary at home for Diwali dismissing a junior and taking perks, sure he has not changed while his brother notices.

passage: Sit, Pooja. You asked why your Vasudha Masi goes quiet in meetings even now. When I was twenty-four, my first boss at the insurance office was a Mr Kulkarni. Each morning, before I opened my mouth, I read his face: a loosened tie meant a good day; a file slammed on the desk meant say nothing. I had ideas, good ones, about the claims backlog. I wrote them in my diary and never said them aloud. When he asked, "Any objections?" I'd smile and say, "It's perfect, sir." Slowly I stopped even noticing my own opinions. I remember walking home feeling small, as if I'd shrunk an inch by evening. That habit stayed long after he retired. So when your manager asks what you think, tell her. Practise while it's cheap.

qa.q: What did a loosened tie mean to Vasudha?
qa.a: A loosened tie meant a good day.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel walking home in the evenings?
qa.a: Vasudha felt small, as if she'd shrunk an inch by evening, after hiding her views all day 😔

qa.q: What choice does Vasudha want Pooja to make that she did not?
qa.a: Vasudha wants Pooja to answer honestly when the manager asks for an opinion, practising while it's cheap, instead of learning to go quiet.

qa.q: What would change if Mr Kulkarni had welcomed objections?
qa.a: Vasudha's ideas on the claims backlog might have been heard, and she might not have carried the habit of silence for years.

grounding: An aunt recalls learning to read a powerful boss's moods, hide her views and shrink, as a young insurance employee.

passage: The slab had to be poured before the rain, and Hemant sir was in one of his moods. Raghav, twenty-four and eight months into the job, could tell from the way his boss chewed the pen cap: a fast chew meant anyone who spoke would be shouted at in front of the labourers. Raghav had spotted a sagging prop under the east corner of the shuttering. He rehearsed the sentence three times in his head. "Sir, the east corner..." Hemant turned. "What? Speak or move." "Nothing, sir. All ready." Raghav went and quietly wedged in an extra prop himself, hands shaking, as the first drops fell. The slab held. Nobody knew. That night on the bus Raghav realised he hadn't said one full sentence of his own all week.

qa.q: What did a fast chew on the pen cap mean?
qa.a: A fast chew meant anyone who spoke would be shouted at in front of the labourers.

qa.q: Why did Raghav say "Nothing, sir. All ready."?
qa.a: Raghav was afraid of being shouted at in front of the labourers, so fear of Hemant's mood swallowed the warning about the sagging prop.

qa.q: What went wrong at the key moment, and what could Raghav try next time?
qa.a: Raghav's warning died under Hemant's impatience; next time Raghav could lead with the plain fact, "The east corner prop is sagging," or tell another engineer so safety doesn't rest on one silent fix.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant asked the team for problems before a pour?
qa.a: Raghav could raise a sagging prop openly, and the site would not depend on a scared junior quietly fixing it in the rain.

grounding: Shows a junior engineer under deadline and rain reading a boss's moods and swallowing a warning, feeling he has lost his own voice.

passage: Every morning at the Andheri office, Kashish checked two things before logging in: the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat. A cheerful "Morning, team!" meant she could ask for the leave she needed. A bare "Status?" meant keep your head down. Six months in, she had learned to rewrite her reports so the bad numbers sat at the bottom, softened. In meetings she waited to see which way Sachin leaned, then agreed. When he called her idea for the client deck "cute", she laughed along and deleted the slide. At home her flatmate asked what she thought about the new project. Kashish opened her mouth and found she didn't know anymore; she only knew what Sachin thought.

qa.q: What two things did Kashish check every morning before logging in?
qa.a: Kashish checked the weather and Sachin's first message in the team chat.

qa.q: What does Kashish's blank moment with her flatmate show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows Kashish has muted her own voice so long that she feels unsure of her own opinion and only knows Sachin's.

qa.q: What small choice could help Kashish get her own view back?
qa.a: Kashish could write down her own opinion before each meeting and keep one honest line about the bad numbers near the top of her reports.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Kashish, compared with what she actually thinks?
qa.a: Sachin probably sees an agreeable employee with no objections, not knowing her real ideas and doubts are hidden to please him.

grounding: Illustrates a junior employee watching a manager's moods, hiding her views and losing touch with her own opinions.

passage: I'm Sarika. When Irawati became our team lead in March, I was the first to hug her. By June something had shifted. She interrupted me twice in one stand-up, finished my sentences wrong, and began expecting the corner parking spot and first pick of leave dates. The others muttered about it in the pantry. I didn't join in, though I was tempted. I also knew her targets had doubled and her own boss called her at night. So one evening, walking to the bus stop, I said, "Ira, you've been cutting people off lately. I think the pressure's getting to you, but it's landing on us." She was quiet for a long stretch. Then: "I didn't realise. Will you tell me when I do it?" Looking back, I'm glad I said it to her and not about her.

qa.q: When did Irawati become the team lead?
qa.a: Irawati became our team lead in March.

qa.q: Why didn't Sarika join the muttering in the pantry?
qa.a: Sarika was tempted but felt sympathy for Irawati, knowing her targets had doubled and her boss called her at night.

qa.q: What choice did Sarika make on the walk to the bus stop, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sarika named the interrupting directly and kindly to Irawati while mentioning the pressure, so Irawati could hear it and asked to be told next time.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt hearing about the change?
qa.a: Irawati was probably surprised and a little stung, going quiet, but also open enough to ask Sarika to tell her when it happens 🙂

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a friend-turned-manager interrupting and taking perks, and naming it gently while crediting the pressure.

passage:
Note, 14 Aug. Devika, Class 3 teacher.
Manjula took over as primary coordinator in June. Things I've noticed since, written down so I don't turn them into staffroom gossip: she cut Rekha off mid-sentence twice at Monday's meeting; she no longer asks us before changing the exam timetable; yesterday she sent the peon to fetch her lunch first, ahead of everyone. The Manjula who shared my tiffin last year would have hated that. I also know the principal emails her at midnight and parents call her personal number.
What I did next: I asked her for tea after school, just the two of us. I said, "You've been interrupting people lately, and it's being noticed. I know you're being squeezed from above." She teared up a little, then laughed. She's asked me to nudge her ankle under the table at the next meeting.

qa.q: When did Manjula take over as primary coordinator?
qa.a: Manjula took over as primary coordinator in June.

qa.q: Why did Devika write the changes down?
qa.a: Devika wanted to keep track of what had changed without turning it into staffroom gossip, which shows a wish to be fair to Manjula.

qa.q: Which choice did Devika make instead of complaining, and how did it land?
qa.a: Devika asked Manjula for tea alone and named the interrupting while acknowledging the pressure; Manjula teared up, laughed, and asked for a nudge under the table.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha when Manjula cuts in mid-sentence?
qa.a: Rekha is likely to feel brushed aside and less willing to speak at meetings, which is part of why Devika's note matters.

grounding: A teacher's note records a friend-turned-coordinator starting to interrupt and expect special treatment, and a gentle private conversation.

passage:
12 Nov. Long day. Rajni's been floor manager for two months and today it really showed. In the huddle she talked over Gurpreet three times and then said, "Let's not waste time on feelings." She also took the window seat by the heater again, the one we used to take turns on. Old Rajni would have rolled her eyes at a manager like this. Ankit tried to get me to moan about her at the chai stall. I didn't. It's not fair either; she has the quality team breathing down her neck and a target that keeps going up. So at clock-out I waited and said, "Raj, you've stopped listening a bit. I get the pressure. I just miss you asking." She went quiet, then said, "Okay. Ouch. Fair." We shared an auto home. I think it landed.

passage:
Subject: a favour, and an honest one
Dear Noor,
You know I've been leading the new library project in Srinagar for a month now. People have started laughing at my jokes a little too hard, and that scares me. So here's the favour: stay the friend who tells me when I'm wrong. You did it in college about my terrible debate speech, and you were right.
A few things I'm trying. Every Friday I ask the team one question: what did my decisions this week cost you? Last week Imran said the new hours meant he missed his daughter's bedtime. We changed them. When the district officer praised the reading corner, I made sure he knew Shazia built it.
If I start sounding pleased with myself, say so. Please.
With love, and a thick skin,
Hafsa

qa.q: What question does Hafsa ask the team every Friday?
qa.a: Hafsa asks: what did my decisions this week cost you?

qa.q: Why does Hafsa feel scared when people laugh at the jokes too hard?
qa.a: Hafsa worries it means people are starting to please the leader instead of being honest, the first step toward self-importance.

qa.q: What did Hafsa change after Imran spoke up, and what does that choice show?
qa.a: Hafsa changed the new hours after Imran said he missed his daughter's bedtime, showing the Friday question leads to real action.

qa.q: How might Shazia feel when the district officer learns who built the reading corner?
qa.a: Shazia would likely feel seen and valued, since Hafsa passed the credit on instead of keeping the praise.

grounding: A young project leader's email asks a friend for honest pushback and describes asking what decisions cost the team and sharing credit.

passage: Okay, Anirban, the honest version. When I became head guide for the Yuksom treks at twenty-four, the porters and younger guides started calling me Dolma-la, and I liked it more than I should have. Then one morning Pemba, my friend since school, said, 'You didn't ask anyone before changing the camp site.' It stung. He was right. So I made rules for myself. Before a big decision, I ask the porters what it costs them: heavier loads, extra walking. I keep Pemba and two others who argue with me close, and I thank them when they do. When a group writes a nice review, I read it out at dinner with every name in it. It's not saintliness. I watched the guide before me slowly stop hearing people, and I don't want that drift.

qa.q: What did Pemba say one morning?
qa.a: Pemba said, 'You didn't ask anyone before changing the camp site.'

qa.q: How did Dolma feel about Pemba's remark?
qa.a: It stung, but Dolma felt Pemba was right, after admitting to liking the title Dolma-la more than was wise.

qa.q: Which of Dolma's habits turned that sting into lasting change?
qa.a: Asking porters what a decision costs them, keeping friends who argue close, and reading reviews aloud with every name keep Dolma listening instead of drifting.

qa.q: How might the porters see Dolma asking them before a big decision?
qa.a: The porters are likely to feel respected and freer to speak honestly, since their loads and extra walking now count 🙂

grounding: A young head guide tells how they invite disagreement, weigh costs to porters and share credit to avoid drifting into self-importance.

passage:
I've worked beside Shankar at the bus depot workshop for three years, so when he was made shift in-charge at twenty-five, I waited to see what would happen. Some people change overnight. Shankar didn't, or not that I could see. The first week he pinned a sheet on the notice board: 'What's one thing I got wrong this week? Drop it in the box, no names.' I thought it was for show. But on Monday he read two of them out and changed the tea-break roster because of one. When the depot manager praised the quick repair of bus 42, Shankar pointed at old Yellappa and me. He still eats lunch on the same bench. I can't tell you what goes on in his head; maybe he's scared of becoming like the last in-charge. From outside, it just looks like he keeps asking.
— Lokesh
